questions.question: Measured over every single flipped bit, how do a sum, an exclusive or, CRC-8 and CRC-16 compare?
options: All four catch every one, so a single bit flip is no reason to choose between them
Only the CRCs catch them
Only CRC-16 catches them all
The sum catches the fewest
questions.explanation: The argument for a CRC has to be made on something other than single bit errors, which is where most of the folklore about it stops.

questions.question: Two bytes of a message are swapped and no bits change. What fraction does a sum catch?
options: None, and this is arithmetic rather than luck, because addition is commutative
About half
All of them, since the positions differ
It depends on the values
questions.explanation: No width of sum fixes it. It is a property of the arithmetic, and it is exactly what a parser locked onto a false start byte produces: correct bytes in the wrong places.

questions.question: Over three million messages, CRC-16 missed zero two byte bursts and about forty five three byte bursts. Why the difference?
options: A CRC of width n detects every burst of n bits or fewer by construction, and above that width it is down to chance at one in two to the n
Three byte bursts are more likely to look like valid data
The polynomial is only defined for short bursts
It is measurement noise, the two rows are the same
questions.explanation: Below the width it is a guarantee, above it every scheme of that width performs the same, which is why sum, exclusive or and CRC-8 all missed about one in 256 of the longer bursts.

questions.question: Your CRC-8 round trips perfectly against your own decoder. What does that prove?
options: Nothing about agreeing with anyone else, since every wrong variant is self consistent too
That the polynomial is correct
That the starting value is correct
That the implementation is standard
questions.explanation: The published check value is what settles it: CRC-8 over the nine bytes 123456789 is 0xF4. Without that you have a checksum that talks to itself.

questions.question: A link is rejecting a steady two percent of frames on their checksum. What is that telling you?
options: Something physical, such as a cable, a ground or a baud rate, and it is saying so before anything else notices
That the checksum is too weak
That the sender is faulty and should be replaced
Nothing useful, some loss is normal
questions.explanation: Counting the failures and reporting the count turns the checksum into a diagnostic instead of only a filter, which is most of its value in the field.

questions.question: You need one wrong message accepted every few hours rather than every few minutes on a busy link. What decides that?
options: The width of the checksum, since above its width every scheme of that width is one in two to the n
The choice of polynomial
Whether the bits are reflected
The starting value
questions.explanation: Eight bits is one in 256 and sixteen is one in 65536. Choose the width from the residual risk you will accept, then choose a standard polynomial of that width so the other end can be told which by name.
